doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Making the artist's record: Laura Nyro and having a sound
summary: Until Laura Nyro's Eli in 1968 he made Calello records; he then learned to serve the song, and discusses Nelson Riddle's recognizable sound.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Am I correct that you would not change your arranging style if you were also the producer?

This – that’s a very interesting question because up until 1968 I made Charlie Calello records. I went in and did Charlie Calello. I didn’t know I was doing it but I’d get called and I’d do this. This is what I did. The first time I realized I had to make somebody else’s record was when I did the Laura Nyro “Eli” record. I met with Laura and she was very, very different. She wrote songs where in the middle of the song the feel would change. The tempo would change. She’d slow down. She’d play songs that didn’t need instruments. And then they’d need something. And I figured out that in order for me to make her record I had to find out what the songs really, really needed. And that was the start of getting to that point. Now this was ’68. By the ‘70s I had pretty much gotten to the – but I didn’t have the realization that this is what I was doing. But I learned how to take the song and the artist and try to record and not make a Charlie Calello record as much as try to make the artist’s record. It was sort of like if you listen to a Nelson Riddle arrangement, as soon as it starts you could tell it’s Nelson. Just the way he put things together. And later on when he did the record he did for that female singer, I forget her name – he hadn’t made a Sinatra record in a long time. He went and made the same © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

record. There was a thing that he did that made Nelson a brilliant record maker and brilliant arranger. Now I had no idea that when I played my arrangements I had people that recognized that I did Charlie Calello, that recognized that -- I didn’t know that I had a sound but there were other people that identified the sound. So now if you have that consistency it’s very, very difficult to then come out of that box and suddenly try to make a twist. Now I didn’t know I was really doing that when I went through the process. I appreciated that I had made that adjustment in the way I made records.

I had a quote from you from our conversation a year ago on the phone, you said, “We never got out of the sound box.” But I can’t remember what the context was. I think you’re talking about that. And were you referring to – Linda Ronstadt did a –
Right. Yeah. Nelson Riddle did the Ronstadt record.

I think it’s very interesting that other people heard that you had a sound but you weren’t aware of it. It’s almost like critics naming styles of music but the musicians don’t know. I mean not that they don’t know but musicians were playing bebop but they didn’t call it bebop until the critics did.
